prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A New York Times reporter who was held by the Taliban for seven months has escaped, the newspaper reported Saturday. New York Times reporter David Rohde, shown in 1995, escaped from the Taliban. David Rohde told his wife, Kristen Mulvihill, that he and a local reporter, Tahir Ludin, climbed over the wall of a compound late Friday where they were being held in the North Waziristan region of Pakistan. Pakistani military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that the Pakistani military was involved in freeing Rohde. Additional details were not immediately available. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton issued a statement expressing her relief about Rohde's "return to freedom." "I would like to thank the governments of Pakistan and Afghanistan for their assistance in ensuring his safe return," Clinton said. "Journalists put themselves at risk every day to report the news in regions gripped by conflict. We rely on their vital role and I am grateful for their service."  Watch CNN's Nic Robertson report on the escape » . Rohde, Ludin and their driver were kidnapped outside of Kabul, Afghanistan, on November 10, and Afghan and Western officials said recently that Rohde was being held in Pakistan. After leaving the compound Friday night, the two men then found a Pakistani army scout who led them to a nearby army base. On Saturday, they were flown to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, the newspaper said. A U.S. official told CNN that Rohde will arrive in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates at 10 p.m. Saturday. "They just walked over the wall of the compound," Mulvihill said, according to the newspaper. Ludin hurt his foot during the escape, but otherwise both men appear to be in good health, the newspaper said. The driver, Asadullah Mangal, did not escape, the newspaper said. "It is hard to describe the enormous relief we felt at hearing the news of David and Tahir's escape and knowing he is safe," a statement from Rohde's family said. "Every day during these past seven months, we have hoped and prayed for this moment," said the statement, which was provided to CNN by The New York Times . It asked that the family's privacy be respected. White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said the White House was "very pleased to see that David Rohde is now safe and returning home." "This marks the end of a long and difficult ordeal for David's family, friends and co-workers. The FBI has been the lead agency on his case, and we refer you to them for any further information," he said. The New York Times and other media outlets had kept the kidnapping quiet out of concern for the men's safety. "From the early days of this ordeal, the prevailing view among David's family, experts in kidnapping cases, officials of several governments and others we consulted, was that going public could increase the danger to hostages," The New York Times said in a written statement. "Therefore, we did not publicly discuss the kidnapping. We are deeply grateful to the other news organizations that honored our request to refrain from reporting on it." A Taliban spokesman told CNN several weeks ago that the Taliban had released two "proof of identity" videos and had demanded negotiations. The Taliban wanted some of its leaders in U.S. custody to be released as well as money, the spokesman said. Rohde, 41, had traveled to Kabul in early November to work on a book, The New York Times said. He won a Pulitzer Prize in 1996 for his reporting on the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia while working for The Christian Science Monitor. He was also part of The New York Times reporting team that won a Pulitzer Prize in May for coverage of Afghanistan and Pakistan last year.

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** A New York Times reporter held captive by the Taliban for seven months has escaped, the newspaper reported Saturday.

David Rohde, pictured in 1995, told his wife, Kristen Mulvihill, that he and a local reporter, Tahir Ludin, climbed over the wall of the compound where they were being held late Friday in Pakistan’s North Waziristan region.

Pakistani military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that the Pakistani military was involved in freeing Rohde. Additional details were not immediately available.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton issued a statement expressing relief over Rohde’s “return to freedom.”

“I would like to thank the governments of Pakistan and Afghanistan for their assistance in ensuring his safe return,” Clinton said. “Journalists put themselves at risk every day to report the news in regions gripped by conflict. We rely on their vital role, and I am grateful for their service.”

*Watch CNN’s Nic Robertson report on the escape »*

Rohde, Ludin, and their driver were kidnapped outside Kabul, Afghanistan, on November 10. Afghan and Western officials had recently said that Rohde was being held in Pakistan.

After leaving the compound Friday night, the two men found a Pakistani army scout, who led them to a nearby army base. On Saturday, they were flown to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, according to the newspaper.

A U.S. official told CNN that Rohde would arrive in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, at 10 p.m. Saturday.

“They just walked over the wall of the compound,” Mulvihill said, according to the newspaper.

Ludin injured his foot during the escape, but both men otherwise appeared to be in good health, the newspaper reported. Their driver, Asadullah Mangal, did not escape.

“It is hard to describe the enormous relief we felt at hearing the news of David and Tahir’s escape and knowing he is safe,” Rohde’s family said in a statement. “Every day during these past seven months, we have hoped and prayed for this moment.”

The statement, provided to CNN by The New York Times, also asked that the family’s privacy be respected.

White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said the White House was “very pleased to see that David Rohde is now safe and returning home.”

“This marks the end of a long and difficult ordeal for David’s family, friends and co-workers. The FBI has been the lead agency on his case, and we refer you to them for any further information,” Gibbs said.

The New York Times and other media organizations had refrained from reporting the kidnapping out of concern for the men’s safety.

“From the early days of this ordeal, the prevailing view among David’s family, experts in kidnapping cases, officials of several governments and others we consulted, was that going public could increase the danger to hostages,” The New York Times said in a written statement. “Therefore, we did not publicly discuss the kidnapping. We are deeply grateful to the other news organizations that honored our request to refrain from reporting on it.”

Several weeks ago, a Taliban spokesman told CNN that the group had released two “proof of identity” videos and demanded negotiations. The spokesman said the Taliban wanted some of its leaders in U.S. custody to be released, as well as money.

Rohde, 41, had traveled to Kabul in early November to work on a book, according to The New York Times.

He won a Pulitzer Prize in 1996 for his reporting on the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia while working for The Christian Science Monitor. He was also part of the New York Times reporting team that won a Pulitzer Prize in May for its coverage of Afghanistan and Pakistan the previous year.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — The New York Times said Saturday that one of its journalists, who had spent seven months in Taliban captivity, had escaped.

David Rohde—pictured in a 1995 image—told his wife, Kristen Mulvihill, that he and Afghan journalist Tahir Ludin scaled the wall of the compound where they were detained late Friday. The facility was in Pakistan’s North Waziristan region.

Pakistani military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that Pakistan’s armed forces had played a role in securing Rohde’s freedom, although no further information was immediately provided.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said she was relieved that Rohde had regained his freedom. She thanked the Pakistani and Afghan governments for helping ensure his safe return and praised journalists who risk their lives to cover conflicts, noting the importance of their work and expressing gratitude for their service.

CNN correspondent Nic Robertson reported on the escape.

Rohde, Ludin and their driver, Asadullah Mangal, were abducted outside Kabul, Afghanistan, on November 10. Afghan and Western officials had recently indicated that Rohde was being held in Pakistan.

After getting out of the compound Friday night, Rohde and Ludin encountered a Pakistani army scout, who guided them to a nearby military base. The Times reported that they were flown Saturday to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan. According to a U.S. official who spoke with CNN, Rohde was scheduled to arrive in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, at 10 p.m. Saturday.

Mulvihill told the newspaper that the two men had simply climbed over the compound wall. Ludin injured his foot while escaping, but both men otherwise appeared healthy, according to the Times. Mangal did not manage to get away.

In a statement supplied to CNN by The New York Times, Rohde’s family said their relief at learning that David and Tahir had escaped—and that David was safe—was almost impossible to put into words. The family said it had spent each day of the previous seven months hoping and praying for such an outcome and requested privacy.

White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said officials were extremely pleased that Rohde was safe and on his way home. He described the escape as the conclusion of a lengthy and painful experience for Rohde’s relatives, friends and colleagues. Gibbs added that the FBI had served as the lead agency in the case and directed requests for additional details to the bureau.

The New York Times and other news organizations had chosen not to report the abduction because they feared publicity could put the captives in greater danger. In a written statement, the Times said that, from the beginning, Rohde’s family, kidnapping specialists, representatives of several governments and other advisers generally agreed that public attention might heighten the risks. For that reason, the paper did not discuss the case publicly and expressed deep appreciation to other media organizations that complied with its request not to cover the kidnapping.

Several weeks before the escape, a Taliban representative told CNN that the group had distributed two videos intended to prove the captives’ identities and had called for negotiations. According to the spokesman, the Taliban sought both money and the release of some of its leaders held by the United States.

Rohde, 41, had gone to Kabul in early November to work on a book, the Times said. While employed by The Christian Science Monitor, he received a Pulitzer Prize in 1996 for his coverage of the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia. He was also a member of the New York Times team awarded a Pulitzer Prize in May for its reporting during the previous year on Afghanistan and Pakistan.

After getting away, the two men encountered a Pakistani army scout who guided them to a nearby military base. Pakistani officials later said the country’s military had been involved in securing Rohde’s freedom.

Rohde, Ludin, and their driver, Asadullah Mangal, had been kidnapped outside Kabul, Afghanistan, on November 10. Ludin injured his foot during the escape, but both reporters were otherwise reported to be in good health. Mangal, however, remained in captivity.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton expressed relief at Rohde’s release and thanked the governments of Pakistan and Afghanistan for their assistance in ensuring his safe return.
outputs.L4:
New York Times reporter David Rohde and Afghan journalist Tahir Ludin escaped after more than seven months in Taliban captivity, climbing over the wall of a compound in Pakistan and making their way to a nearby Pakistani military position. There, they encountered an army scout who helped bring them to safety.

Rohde and Ludin had been abducted in Afghanistan in November 2008 while traveling to interview a Taliban commander. Their captors later moved them across the border into Pakistan’s tribal region, where they were held under close guard. A third captive, their driver, Asadullah Mangal, did not escape with them.

Both journalists were reported to be in good health following their ordeal, although Ludin injured his foot during the escape. News of their freedom brought relief to their families, colleagues and press-freedom advocates around the world. The episode also highlighted the severe risks faced by reporters and local media workers covering insurgencies and other conflicts, where kidnapping, violence and prolonged detention remain persistent threats.
